questions.stem: The SI unit of frequency is the
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, so its unit is $\text{s}^{-1}$, which is given the special name hertz. One hertz is one complete wave per second.

distractorRationale.a: The second is the unit of period, the reciprocal of frequency
distractorRationale.c: The metre is the unit of wavelength and amplitude
distractorRationale.d: Metre per second is the unit of wave speed

questions.stem: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate

options.text: parallel to the direction of travel of the wave
perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave
only when the wave reaches a boundary

questions.explanation: A transverse wave is defined by vibration at right angles to the direction of energy transfer, which is what produces the familiar pattern of crests and troughs. Waves on a rope and light waves are transverse.

distractorRationale.a: Vibration along the direction of travel defines a longitudinal wave, such as sound
distractorRationale.c: Circular particle motion occurs in deep-water waves as a special case, not as the definition of transverse
distractorRationale.d: Particles vibrate everywhere the wave passes, not only at boundaries

questions.stem: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
questions.explanation: Sound travels through air as a series of compressions and rarefactions in which the air molecules oscillate back and forth along the direction the sound is travelling. That makes it longitudinal, and it is also why sound cannot cross a vacuum.

distractorRationale.a: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, which is why it can be polarised
distractorRationale.b: Radio waves are electromagnetic and therefore transverse
distractorRationale.d: A rope wave moves up and down while the energy travels along the rope, so it is transverse

questions.stem: A vibrator produces water waves of frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4.0 m. Calculate the speed of the waves. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 4.0 = 200\ \text{m/s}$. Because hertz is per second, multiplying by a length in metres gives metres per second directly.

questions.stem: A sound wave of frequency 680 Hz travels through air at 340 m/s. Calculate its wavelength. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: Rearranging the wave equation gives $\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340}{680} = 0.50\ \text{m}$. High-frequency sounds have short wavelengths, and low-frequency sounds long ones, for a fixed speed.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz. Calculate its period. Give your answer in seconds.
questions.explanation: $T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{25} = 0.040\ \text{s}$. Period and frequency are reciprocals, so a high frequency always means a short period.

questions.stem: When a wave passes from one medium into another, which of its properties does NOT change?
questions.explanation: Frequency is fixed by the vibrating source, which does not change when the wave crosses a boundary. The new medium alters the speed, so from $v = f\lambda$ the wavelength must adjust instead. This is precisely why refraction bends a wave.

distractorRationale.a: Speed depends on the properties of the medium, so it changes at a boundary
distractorRationale.b: Wavelength changes in proportion to the speed because the frequency is fixed
distractorRationale.d: Direction changes unless the wave strikes the boundary along the normal

questions.stem: The amplitude of a wave is a measure of

options.text: the number of waves passing a point per second
the distance between two successive crests
the energy carried by the wave
the speed at which the wave travels

questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position, and the energy a wave carries is proportional to the square of the amplitude. A louder sound or a brighter light corresponds to a larger amplitude, not to a different frequency.

distractorRationale.d: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on how large the oscillations are

questions.stem: A wave of period 0.020 s travels through a medium at 300 m/s. Calculate its wavelength. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: First convert the period to a frequency: $f = \frac{1}{0.020} = 50\ \text{Hz}$. Then $\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{300}{50} = 6.0\ \text{m}$. A quicker route is $\lambda = vT = 300 \times 0.020 = 6.0\ \text{m}$, since the wave advances one wavelength in one period.

questions.stem: A source makes 300 complete vibrations in one minute, producing waves of wavelength 0.80 m. Calculate the speed of the waves. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: First find the frequency in vibrations per second: $f = \frac{300}{60} = 5.0\ \text{Hz}$. Then $v = f\lambda = 5.0 \times 0.80 = 4.0\ \text{m/s}$. Using 300 as the frequency without converting the minute to seconds would give an answer sixty times too large.
